blocks.text: A steel gear is sealed in a furnace at 930 degrees C in a carbon-rich gas for several hours, and afterwards its surface is hard to 1 mm deep while its core stays tough. The carbon moved only because atoms in a solid hop between sites, and that movement can be calculated.

blocks.markdown: Atoms in a crystal are not frozen. Thermal vibration occasionally lets an atom jump to an adjacent vacant site, and in a concentration gradient more atoms jump down the gradient than up it, producing a net flow called **diffusion**. This unit gives the equations for the flow (Fick's laws), how fast it goes (the temperature dependence of $D$), and one important application (carburising).

blocks.title: Flux and diffusion coefficient
blocks.text: Flux $J$ is the quantity of diffusing species crossing unit area per unit time, in kg/(m$^2$ s) or atoms/(m$^2$ s). The diffusion coefficient $D$, in m$^2$/s, is the proportionality between flux and concentration gradient $\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$ ($C$ in kg/m$^3$, $x$ in m).

blocks.caption: Fick's first law. The minus sign means flow is down the concentration gradient. Valid when the profile does not change with time (steady state).

blocks.title: Steady-state hydrogen leak through a vessel wall
blocks.prompt: A thin steel wall 2.0 mm thick has hydrogen concentrations $C_1=2.0$ kg/m$^3$ on the high-pressure face and $C_2=0.4$ kg/m$^3$ on the other. The diffusion coefficient is assumed to be $1.0\times10^{-9}$ m$^2$/s. Find the flux.

steps.text: In steady state the gradient is uniform, so $\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x=(C_2-C_1)/\Delta x$.

blocks.answer: $J=8.0\times10^{-7}$ kg/(m$^2$ s), directed from the high-concentration face to the low one.

blocks.markdown: **Time-dependent diffusion.** When the profile changes with time, Fick's second law, $\partial C/\partial t=D\,\partial^2C/\partial x^2$, applies. For a semi-infinite solid with initial uniform concentration $C_0$ and a constant surface concentration $C_s$, which models carburising, the solution is

blocks.caption: $C_x$: concentration at depth $x$ and time $t$; erf is the error function, tabulated in the table below.

blocks.markdown: **Temperature dependence.** Diffusion is thermally activated. Only atoms with energy above the activation energy $Q_d$ (J/mol) can make a jump, and the diffusion coefficient follows an Arrhenius law,

blocks.caption: $D_0$: pre-exponential factor (m$^2$/s); $R=8.314$ J/(mol K); $T$ in kelvin.

blocks.title: Carburising time for a target case depth
blocks.prompt: A steel with 0.20 wt% C is carburised at 950 degrees C ($T=1223$ K) with the surface held at $C_s=1.00$ wt% C. Typical values for carbon in FCC iron are $D_0=2.3\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s and $Q_d=148$ kJ/mol. How long is needed to reach 0.60 wt% C at a depth of 0.50 mm?

steps.text: Left side of the erf solution.
From tables, $\operatorname{erf}(z)=0.50$ gives $z=0.477$ (interpolating between 0.4284 at 0.4 and 0.5205 at 0.5).

items: Depth for a given concentration grows as $\sqrt{Dt}$: doubling the depth needs four times the time.
A small rise in temperature raises $D$ strongly, so carburising is done hot (about 900 to 950 degrees C), where steel is FCC austenite and dissolves much more carbon than BCC ferrite.
Steady-state problems use Fick's first law; changing-profile problems use the erf solution.
Always convert thickness and depth to metres, temperature to kelvin and use consistent $R$.

blocks.title: Which equation when?
blocks.text: If the concentration at every point is constant in time, use $J=D(C_1-C_2)/\Delta x$. If a surface is held at fixed concentration and atoms move in, use the error-function solution. If $D$ changes with temperature, use the Arrhenius form first.

points: Fick's first law, $J=-D\,\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$, gives flux for steady-state diffusion; through a thin plate $J=D\Delta C/\Delta x$.
$D=D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT)$, so $\ln D$ against $1/T$ has slope $-Q_d/R$ and $D$ at a new temperature follows from the ratio form.
The erf solution gives the concentration profile when a surface is held at $C_s$, and case depth scales as $\sqrt{Dt}$.

questions.stem: In Fick's first law, $J=-D\,\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$, why is there a minus sign?

options.text: Because net flux is directed from high concentration to low concentration, opposite to the concentration gradient
Because diffusion always removes atoms from the material
Because $D$ is a negative number for diffusing species
Because the flux is measured in the direction of increasing temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Because net flux is directed from high concentration to low concentration, opposite to the concentration gradient

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the gradient points up the concentration hill, the flux down it.
distractorRationale.b: Diffusion redistributes atoms; it does not remove them from a closed system.
distractorRationale.c: $D$ is always positive; the sign belongs to the gradient.
distractorRationale.d: Fick's first law relates flux to concentration gradient; temperature enters only through $D$.

questions.explanation: The concentration gradient $\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$ is positive when concentration increases with $x$, but atoms migrate toward lower concentration, so the flux has the opposite sign. $D$ is positive and sets only how fast this evening-out occurs.

questions.stem: In steady-state diffusion through a thin plate of constant diffusion coefficient, the concentration varies linearly with position through the thickness.
questions.explanation: Steady state means the flux $J$ is the same at every position and constant in time. With $J=-D\,\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$ and constant $D$, the gradient must then be constant, so $C$ is linear in $x$.

questions.stem: The diffusion coefficient follows $D=D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT)$. What happens to $D$ when the absolute temperature is raised?

options.text: It increases exponentially, and increases proportionally faster when $Q_d$ is larger
It decreases because atoms collide more often
It is independent of $T$ and depends only on concentration

questions.correctOptionText: It increases exponentially, and increases proportionally faster when $Q_d$ is larger

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the Arrhenius form means a larger activation energy makes $D$ more temperature sensitive.
distractorRationale.b: The dependence is exponential in $1/T$, not linear.
distractorRationale.c: More thermal energy lets more atoms overcome the barrier $Q_d$, so $D$ rises.
distractorRationale.d: $D$ depends strongly on temperature; this is the basis of thermally activated processes.

questions.explanation: Diffusion is thermally activated: an atom must acquire the energy $Q_d$ to jump into the neighbouring site, and the fraction of atoms with that energy rises as $\exp(-Q_d/RT)$. A higher $Q_d$ means a steeper rise of $D$ with temperature.

questions.stem: A polymer film 0.50 mm thick separates two chambers. A solute has concentration 1.2 kg/m$^3$ on one face and 0.2 kg/m$^3$ on the other face, and its diffusion coefficient in the film is $3.0\times10^{-11}$ m$^2$/s. Assuming steady state, calculate the flux in units of $10^{-8}$ kg/(m$^2$ s).
questions.explanation: Steady-state flux is $J=D(C_1-C_2)/\Delta x=3.0\times10^{-11}\times(1.2-0.2)/(0.50\times10^{-3})=6.0\times10^{-8}$ kg/(m$^2$ s). The thickness must be converted to metres before substituting.

questions.stem: A diffusing species has $D=1.0\times10^{-14}$ m$^2$/s at 900 K and an activation energy $Q_d=125$ kJ/mol. Taking $R=8.314$ J/(mol K), calculate $D$ at 1000 K in units of $10^{-14}$ m$^2$/s.
questions.explanation: From the Arrhenius law, $D_2=D_1\exp\left[\frac{Q_d}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right]$. The exponent is $(125000/8.314)(1/900-1/1000)=1.670$, so $D_2=1.0\times10^{-14}\times e^{1.670}=5.3\times10^{-14}$ m$^2$/s.

questions.stem: A steel containing 0.10 wt% C is carburised in an atmosphere that holds the surface at 1.00 wt% C. The diffusion coefficient of carbon at the treatment temperature is $1.6\times10^{-11}$ m$^2$/s. Using the error-function solution, calculate the depth in mm at which the carbon content is 0.40 wt% after 4.0 h.
questions.explanation: The solution is $\frac{C_x-C_0}{C_s-C_0}=1-\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right)$. Here $(0.40-0.10)/(1.00-0.10)=0.333$, so $\mathrm{erf}(z)=0.667$; from tables, $\mathrm{erf}(0.6)=0.6039$ and $\mathrm{erf}(0.7)=0.6778$, so $z=0.684$ by interpolation. Then $x=2z\sqrt{Dt}=2(0.684)\sqrt{1.6\times10^{-11}\times14400}=0.66$ mm.

questions.stem: A carburising treatment gives a case depth of 0.6 mm in 4 h at a fixed temperature and surface carbon content. If the same treatment is run for 16 h, what case depth (to the same carbon level) is expected?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: depth scales as $\sqrt t$, and $\sqrt{16/4}=2$.
distractorRationale.b: This assumes depth is proportional to time, but diffusion depth goes as $\sqrt{t}$.
distractorRationale.c: Case depth keeps growing with time; it does not saturate.
distractorRationale.d: Depth cannot decrease as treatment time increases.

questions.explanation: For a given carbon level, $x/(2\sqrt{Dt})$ is constant, so $x\propto\sqrt{Dt}$. Quadrupling the time doubles the depth, taking 0.6 mm to 1.2 mm; this is why deep cases take disproportionately long.

questions.stem: An Arrhenius plot of $\ln D$ against $1/T$ (with $T$ in kelvin) for a diffusing species is a straight line of slope $-1.5\times10^{4}$ K. Using $R=8.314$ J/(mol K), what is the activation energy?

distractorRationale.b: This reads the slope as an energy directly, without multiplying by $R$.
distractorRationale.c: This divides the slope by $R$ instead of multiplying.
distractorRationale.d: Activation energy is positive; the minus sign belongs to the slope.

questions.explanation: Taking the logarithm of $D=D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT)$ gives $\ln D=\ln D_0-(Q_d/R)(1/T)$, so the slope is $-Q_d/R$. Hence $Q_d=15000\times8.314=1.25\times10^5$ J/mol, or 125 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: State Fick's first law and use it to explain why, for steady-state diffusion of a gas through a thin wall, the flux is inversely proportional to the wall thickness. State the assumptions.
markingGuide: States $J=-D\,\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}x$ with symbols and units defined (2 marks)
Steady state: $J$ is independent of position and time, so the gradient is constant and the profile linear (2 marks)
$J=D(C_1-C_2)/\Delta x$, so doubling the thickness halves the flux for fixed face concentrations (2 marks)
Assumptions: constant $D$ (independent of $C$), fixed concentrations on both faces, one-dimensional flow (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Fick's first law relates flux to the concentration gradient. In steady state with constant $D$ the profile is linear, so the gradient is $(C_1-C_2)/\Delta x$ and flux falls as $1/\Delta x$.

questions.stem: Two gas-carburising runs are planned to reach the same carbon concentration at the same depth. Run A is at 900 degrees C and Run B at 950 degrees C. Using the error-function solution and $D=D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT)$, explain which run is shorter and by roughly what factor, taking $Q_d=148$ kJ/mol, $D_0=2.3\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s.
markingGuide: For fixed surface, initial and target concentrations, $x/(2\sqrt{Dt})$ is a constant, so $Dt$ is the same for both runs (2 marks)
Ratio $D_B/D_A\approx1.86$, so Run B takes about 54 percent of the time of Run A (2 marks)
Mention of the trade-off: higher temperature increases grain growth and distortion (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The target condition fixes $Dt$, so the run with the larger $D$ is shorter. Raising the temperature from 1173 K to 1223 K raises $D$ by about 1.86 times, so the time falls to roughly 0.54 of the original.
